extracted.intended_audience: users of the Magma computer-algebra system (mathematicians and programmers learning Magma)
extracted.subtask_short: writing Magma programs: magmas and conditionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rules for constructing and manipulating magmas, aggregate structures, and control-flow constructs in the Magma language; includes syntax, semantics, performance notes, and recommended idioms. Intended to guide correct and efficient Magma code authoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorthand constructors return natural homomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Like the quo-constructor, shorthand constructors return the natural homomorphism as their second return value; the domain of the homomorphism is always the corresponding free magma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A<x,y,z>, n := AbelianGroup< x, y, z | 2*y=4*x, x+10*y >; then n is a Mapping from the free magma to the quotient. Use this when creating quotient-like shorthand constructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorthand constructors for generic magmas produce submagmas
rubrics_metrics.description: For categories with generic magmas (matrix groups, matrix algebras/rings, permutation groups, linear codes), the shorthand constructor creates a submagma of the generic magma, not a quotient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syntax: constructor-word< generic magma specification | generators >. The left-hand generic specification matches the arguments of the generic constructor (e.g., MatrixGroup<degree, ring | generators>). In most categories the shorthand returns the inclusion monomorphism as second return value.

rubrics_metrics.name: # operator returns magma cardinality
rubrics_metrics.description: If an expression returning a finite magma is preceded by #, Magma returns the cardinality (number of elements) of the magma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For groups, Order(M) is a synonym for #M. Example: #GF(2,4) returns 16.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection operator (L meet M) returns magma intersection preserving axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Given comparable magmas L and M, L meet M returns their intersection — the magma consisting of elements common to both — and the intersection will normally satisfy the same axioms as the original magmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: intersection of two subspaces of a vector space is a subspace. Use meet for set-theoretic intersections that preserve structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set(M) and FormalSet(M) semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Set(M) returns the set of elements of a (small) finite magma M; FormalSet(M) returns the formal set of elements of any magma M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set(M) lists actual elements (usable for small finite magmas). FormalSet(FreeGroup(3)) returns a formal set description rather than enumerating elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rep(M) vs Random(M) element-selection semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Rep(M) returns an arbitrary representative element of M and will return the same representative each time; Random(M) returns a random element (each element equal probability) and may return different elements on repeated calls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random(M) requires M to be finite. Use Rep when a deterministic representative is desired; use Random for sampling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relational operators require comparable operands
rubrics_metrics.description: Relational operators (e.g., eq, ne, in, notin, subset, notsubset) are only available when the operands are comparable (belong to the same magma or have coercion to a common overstructure) and the operator is defined for that overstructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If operands are not comparable, a runtime error will be produced. Example errors: "'in': Bad argument types" for "w" in WittDesign(12) or eq between incompatible magmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: cmpeq operator: safe equality-check without errors
rubrics_metrics.description: cmpeq is similar to eq but never gives an error message if arguments are incomparable; it returns true whenever L eq M would be true, otherwise false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cmpeq to test suitability of arguments in function/procedure invocations where incomparability should be treated as false rather than an error. Example: MatrixRing(GF(2),3) cmpeq Sym(6) returns false (no error).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caching and concise representations for large magmas; prefer built-ins
rubrics_metrics.description: Magma constructs concise representations for large magmas and caches computed information automatically, but calculations on very large magmas can still consume significant time and storage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before writing your own routine to build a standard mathematical object, check whether Magma already provides an operator/function; Magma's version is likely faster due to optimized algorithms and storage techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: if-statement basic form and syntax rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic if-statement form is: if condition then statements else statements end if; statements must end with semicolons. Newlines and indentation are optional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The then-block executes if condition true; else-block executes if false. Use semicolons at the end of statements, and prefer readable indentation for maintainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special prompt symbol for incomplete compound statements
rubrics_metrics.description: While typing an incomplete if/while/for statement, Magma may show the special prompt 'if>' (or analogous) to remind the user the statement has not yet closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control prompt style with SetPrompt(P). The example SetPrompt("> ") yields simple prompt; SetPrompt("%S> ") yields reminder-style prompts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short form of if-statement when no else action needed
rubrics_metrics.description: If no action is needed when the condition is false, use the short form: if condition then statements end if; omitting the else clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this form to simplify code where only the true-case requires action (example shown for absolute-value logic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid nested if-statements by using elif
rubrics_metrics.description: Use elif (else if) clauses to avoid nested if-statements; it removes the need for extra end if closures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syntax: if cond then ... elif cond then ... elif cond then ... else ... end if; Example: converting percentage marks to grades.

rubrics_metrics.name: select-expression for conditional expressions (call-by-name)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select-expression syntax: condition select expr1 else expr2 — evaluates to expr1 if condition true, else expr2. Evaluation is call-by-name (only chosen expression evaluated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when the only action is choosing a value (e.g., assigning y := x ge 0 select x else -x;). Because of call-by-name, side-effects in the unchosen branch are not executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: case-statement semantics (first-match, single block executed)
rubrics_metrics.description: case-statement: evaluate case expression then check when clauses in order; execute statements of the first matching when only. The else clause is optional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple when options match, only the first (from the top) is used. Use case for multi-way branching; example uses Sign(A+B-C) for triangle existence logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: case-expression syntax and semantics (default required, call-by-name)
rubrics_metrics.description: case-expression: case< expr | exprL1:exprR1, ..., default:exprdflt > — evaluate initial expr, compare to exprLi in order, return corresponding exprRi on match; if no match return default. Evaluation is call-by-name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default is compulsory (unlike else in case-statement). Example: mapping mark ranges to grade strings via case< true | mark ge 85 : "High Distinction", ... default: "Fail" >.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate categories and bracketing conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Magma provides many aggregate categories (enumerated sets, multisets, indexed sets, enumerated sequences, formal sets, lists, Cartesian products, tuples, coproducts, record formats, records) distinguished by specific bracketing symbols (e.g., { ... } for enumerated sets, [ ... ] for sequences, {* ... *} for multisets, {@ ... @} for indexed sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Table 6.1 for bracketing symbols. Choose the aggregate category whose semantics (homogeneous/iterable/ordered/repeated) match your needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer enumerated sets and sequences for performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated sets and enumerated sequences are highly optimized in Magma and have many operations available; users should prefer them for aggregate data structures where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated sets are stored in hash tables for fast membership tests; enumerated sequences support many sequence operations. Use these for typical mathematical programming tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneous, iterable, ordered, and repeated-element properties explained
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: homogeneous = all elements have same parent magma (universe); iterable = finite and system can generate elements on demand; ordered = has index map S[1]..S[n]; repeated elements allowed in multisets, sequences, lists, tuples but not in strict sets/indexed sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties determine internal representation and available operations. Iterability implies finite and stored/generable elements; ordered aggregates have indexing starting at 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two main construction methods for iterable homogeneous aggregates
rubrics_metrics.description: Create aggregates either from a list of expressions whose values are the elements, or from an element-description using set-theoretic notation which Magma evaluates. Special construction exists for arithmetic progressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When elements are given literally as primitive sequences, declare the universe explicitly to avoid repeated coercions. For arithmetic progressions, Magma stores only initial/final/common-difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiset multiplicity syntax and Multiplicity function
rubrics_metrics.description: In multiset element lists, the notation e^^m denotes element e with multiplicity m (equivalent to m repetitions). Use Multiplicity(S, x) to get multiplicity of x in multiset S (or 0 if absent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: {* 2, 2, 3, 6, 1, 3, 3, 5, 3 *} prints multiplicities; ms2 := {* (a+4*c)^^4, b+c, ... *}; Multiplicity(ms2, a+4*c) returns 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universe(S) and declaring/changing the universe of aggregates
rubrics_metrics.description: Universe(S) returns the common parent magma (universe) of an aggregate S. You may explicitly declare the universe at construction using syntax { Universe | ... } or change it later via ChangeUniverse(S, U) or ChangeUniverse(~S, U).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit universe declaration is required when intended universe differs from Magma's inferred universe or when elements are specified literally as primitive sequences (to avoid coercion errors). Example: { RationalField() | 6,3,8,2 } allows later inclusion of 7/9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empty vs null aggregates
rubrics_metrics.description: An empty iterable homogeneous aggregate has a declared universe but no elements. A null aggregate has no universe and no elements. IsEmpty(S) tests emptiness; IsNull(S) tests nullness (IsEmpty returns true for null as well).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empty sets restrict what can be inserted later to elements that fit the declared universe; null sets accept any first-inserted element which then defines the universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic-progression aggregate constructors and semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Shorthand notations {i..j}, [i..j], {i..j by k}, [i..j by k] create enumerated sets or sequences as integer arithmetic progressions: {i..j} is set {i, i+1, ..., j}; [i..j] is sequence [i, i+1, ..., j]; with 'by k' step k (k != 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are stored efficiently (virtual collection) rather than listing every element; use them for integer ranges and regular sequences.
